claim: The microfluidic device contains three compartments (presynaptic, synaptic, and postsynaptic) that are fluidically isolated and separated by microchannels.
source: These devices contain three compartments (presynaptic, synaptic, and postsynaptic) that are fluidically isolated and separated by microchannels that are 5 μm high and 5 μm wide, but of two different lengths: 500 μm and 75 μm (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript directly describes the physical structure of the microfluidic device used in the experiments.

claim: The 500 μm channels allow only axons from the presynaptic compartment to reach the synaptic compartment.
source: The 500 μm channels allow only axons from the presynaptic compartment to reach the synaptic compartment (Taylor et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Taylor et al., 2005 and the design of the microfluidic system.

claim: The 75 μm long microchannels allow dendrites to cross from the postsynaptic to the synaptic compartment.
source: The 75 μm long microchannels allow dendrites to cross from the postsynaptic to the synaptic compartment, where MAP2 staining shows they connect with axons coming from the presynaptic compartment (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by MAP2 staining data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Full maturation of the corticocortical neuronal network occurs between days in vitro (DIV) 10 and 15.
source: In these microfluidic devices, we observed full maturation of the corticocortical neuronal network between days in vitro (DIV) 10 and 15, as revealed by uptake of FM4-64, an indicator of endocytosis/exocytosis of functional synapses (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by FM4-64 uptake data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: APP-mCherry retains APP characteristics.
source: We transduced mouse cortical neurons at DIV eight with lentiviruses expressing APP tagged with mCherry at the C terminus (APP-mCherry), which retains APP characteristics (Kaether et al., 2000; Marquer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kaether et al., 2000 and Marquer et al., 2014.

claim: Velocities of APP-mCherry vesicles reach a maximum at DIV13.
source: We recorded the movements of APP-mCherry vesicles at high frequency frame rate using spinning disk confocal microscopy and found that velocities reach a maximum at DIV13, when the network is fully mature, with established synapses (Figure 1B and C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B, 1C, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is a net anterograde axonal flux for APP-mCherry-containing vesicles.
source: Our analysis showed a net anterograde axonal and outward dendritic flux for APP-mCherry-containing vesicles, indicating that there is a significant transport of APP to the synapse from both pre- and postsynaptic neurons (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by kymograph analysis data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: There is a net outward dendritic flux for APP-mCherry-containing vesicles.
source: Our analysis showed a net anterograde axonal and outward dendritic flux for APP-mCherry-containing vesicles, indicating that there is a significant transport of APP to the synapse from both pre- and postsynaptic neurons (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by kymograph analysis data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: APP is transported to the synapse from both pre- and postsynaptic neurons.
source: Our analysis showed a net anterograde axonal and outward dendritic flux for APP-mCherry-containing vesicles, indicating that there is a significant transport of APP to the synapse from both pre- and postsynaptic neurons (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is inferred from the net flux data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Phosphorylation of HTT at Serine 421 determines the direction in which various cargoes are transported in neurites.
source: We had previously shown that phosphorylation of HTT at Serine 421 determines the direction in which various cargoes are transported in neurites (Colin et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Colin et al., 2008.

claim: Neither the S421A nor S421D mutation affects the level of HTT expression.
source: It is important to note that neither mutation affects the level of HTT expression (Ehinger et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ehinger et al., 2020.

claim: Abolishing HTT phosphorylation at Serine 421 increased the velocity of retrograde vesicles.
source: Abolishing HTT phosphorylation at Serine 421 increased the velocity of retrograde vesicles, increased their cumulative distance travelled, and reduced the net anterograde flux of APP vesicles in axons (Figure 3A, Video 3)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and Video 3.

claim: Abolishing HTT phosphorylation at Serine 421 increased the cumulative distance travelled by retrograde vesicles.
source: Abolishing HTT phosphorylation at Serine 421 increased the velocity of retrograde vesicles, increased their cumulative distance travelled, and reduced the net anterograde flux of APP vesicles in axons (Figure 3A, Video 3)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and Video 3.

claim: Abolishing HTT phosphorylation at Serine 421 reduced the net anterograde flux of APP vesicles in axons.
source: Abolishing HTT phosphorylation at Serine 421 increased the velocity of retrograde vesicles, increased their cumulative distance travelled, and reduced the net anterograde flux of APP vesicles in axons (Figure 3A, Video 3)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and Video 3.

claim: HTTSD neurons showed an increase in anterograde velocity compared to HTTSA or wild type neurons.
source: whereas HTTSD neurons showed an increase in anterograde velocity and greater cumulative distance travelled by APP compared to HTTSA or wild type (WT) neurons.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of transport data between genotypes.

claim: HTTSD neurons showed greater cumulative distance travelled by APP compared to HTTSA or wild type neurons.
source: whereas HTTSD neurons showed an increase in anterograde velocity and greater cumulative distance travelled by APP compared to HTTSA or wild type (WT) neurons.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of transport data between genotypes.

claim: Most of the WT HTT is in its phosphorylated form in the experimental conditions.
source: Nevertheless, the net flux, which reflects the flow of vesicles from the soma to axon terminals, was not significantly different from that observed in WT neurons. This indicates that in our experimental conditions, most of the WT HTT is in its phosphorylated form.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity of net flux between HTTSD and WT neurons.

claim: Phosphorylation status of HTT did not modify APP transport in dendrites.
source: Phosphorylation status did not, however, modify APP transport in dendrites (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: HTT phosphorylation regulates axonal but not dendritic transport of APP to the synapse.
source: We conclude that HTT phosphorylation regulates axonal but not dendritic transport of APP to the synapse.
evidence: This is concluded from the differential effects observed in axons versus dendrites.

claim: HTTSA neurons had less KHC in the vesicular fraction than in the cytosolic fraction compared to WT neurons.
source: We found no difference between WT and HTTSA neurons in their total kinesin heavy chain (KHC) levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), but HTTSA neurons had less KHC in the vesicular fraction than in the cytosolic fraction (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: HTT dephosphorylation decreases the association of kinesin-1 with vesicles.
source: These results are in agreement with our previous study suggesting HTT dephosphorylation decreases the association of kinesin-1 with vesicles (Colin et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Colin et al., 2008 and the current vesicular fractionation data.

claim: HTT phosphorylation at S421 depends on the Akt kinase.
source: HTT phosphorylation at S421 depends on the Akt kinase (Humbert et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Humbert et al., 2002.

claim: Akt induced endogenous HTT phosphorylation in WT neurons but was unable to do so in HTTSA neurons.
source: As expected, Akt induced endogenous HTT phosphorylation in WT neurons but was unable to do so in HTTSA neurons (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: HTT phosphorylation was reduced upon Akt-N expression.
source: In addition, HTT phosphorylation was reduced upon Akt-N expression.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data.

claim: Expressing Akt-CA in WT cortical neurons markedly increased anterograde velocity of APP.
source: Expressing Akt-CA and APP-mCherry in WT cortical neurons had no effect on vesicle number but markedly increased anterograde velocity of APP and the cumulative distances travelled by anterograde APP-mCherry-containing vesicles, which in turn led to an increase of their net anterograde flux (Figure 4B and C, Video 4).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B and C, and Video 4.

claim: Expressing Akt-CA in WT cortical neurons increased the cumulative distances travelled by anterograde APP-mCherry-containing vesicles.
source: Expressing Akt-CA and APP-mCherry in WT cortical neurons had no effect on vesicle number but markedly increased anterograde velocity of APP and the cumulative distances travelled by anterograde APP-mCherry-containing vesicles, which in turn led to an increase of their net anterograde flux (Figure 4B and C, Video 4).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B and C, and Video 4.

claim: Expressing Akt-CA in WT cortical neurons led to an increase of net anterograde flux of APP vesicles.
source: Expressing Akt-CA and APP-mCherry in WT cortical neurons had no effect on vesicle number but markedly increased anterograde velocity of APP and the cumulative distances travelled by anterograde APP-mCherry-containing vesicles, which in turn led to an increase of their net anterograde flux (Figure 4B and C, Video 4).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B and C, and Video 4.

claim: In HTTSA neurons, Akt-CA was unable to modify the different transport parameters.
source: In contrast, in HTTSA neurons, Akt-CA was unable to modify the different transport parameters.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of transport data in HTTSA neurons with and without Akt-CA.

claim: Akt activation increases APP anterograde transport in axons by phosphorylating HTT at Serine 421.
source: Thus, Akt activation increases APP anterograde transport in axons by phosphorylating HTT at Serine 421.
evidence: This is concluded from the differential effects of Akt-CA in WT versus HTTSA neurons.

claim: Akt-HTT signaling is a new mechanism that regulates axonal trafficking of APP.
source: These results identify Akt-HTT signaling as a new mechanism that regulates axonal trafficking of APP.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined data on Akt and HTT phosphorylation effects on APP transport.

claim: Cells expressing pARIS HTTSA had far fewer APP-SEP dots per minute than cells expressing pARIS HTT.
source: We detected far fewer APP-SEP dots per minute in cells expressing pARIS HTTSA than in cells expressing pARIS HTT (Figure 5A, Video 5).
evidence: This is supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 5A and Video 5.

claim: Reducing transport of APP to the plasma membrane by dephosphorylating HTT decreases APP targeting at the plasma membrane.
source: This result suggests that reducing transport of APP to the plasma membrane by dephosphorylating HTT decreases APP targeting at the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is inferred from the TIRF microscopy data showing reduced exocytosis events.

claim: Lack of HTT phosphorylation led to a reduction of APP protein levels at synapses.
source: Lack of HTT phosphorylation led to a reduction of APP protein levels at synapses but no real change in the soma-containing chamber (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data from synaptic chamber shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Most of the synaptosomal APP was enriched in the non-PSD fraction.
source: We detected APP in both fractions. We found that most of the synaptosomal APP was enriched in the non-PSD fraction, which suggests that a significant fraction of APP found at synapses originates from the presynaptic compartment.
evidence: This is supported by synaptosomal fractionation data.

claim: A significant fraction of APP found at synapses originates from the presynaptic compartment.
source: We detected APP in both fractions. We found that most of the synaptosomal APP was enriched in the non-PSD fraction, which suggests that a significant fraction of APP found at synapses originates from the presynaptic compartment.
evidence: This is inferred from the enrichment of APP in the non-PSD (presynaptic) fraction.

claim: APP levels were lower in the non-PSD fraction of HTTSA mouse brains.
source: APP levels were lower in the non-PSD fraction of HTTSA mouse brains (enriched with presynaptic proteins), but APP levels did not differ significantly between WT and HTTSA mouse brains in the PSD fraction (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: APP levels did not differ significantly between WT and HTTSA mouse brains in the PSD fraction.
source: APP levels were lower in the non-PSD fraction of HTTSA mouse brains (enriched with presynaptic proteins), but APP levels did not differ significantly between WT and HTTSA mouse brains in the PSD fraction (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The absence of HTT phosphorylation reduces anterograde transport of APP in axons, but not in dendrites.
source: Together, our results indicate that the absence of HTT phosphorylation reduces anterograde transport of APP in axons, but not in dendrites, and subsequently regulates the levels of APP in the presynaptic compartment both in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined in vitro and in vivo data.

claim: The absence of HTT phosphorylation regulates the levels of APP in the presynaptic compartment both in vitro and in vivo.
source: Together, our results indicate that the absence of HTT phosphorylation reduces anterograde transport of APP in axons, but not in dendrites, and subsequently regulates the levels of APP in the presynaptic compartment both in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined in vitro and in vivo data.

claim: HTTSA mice at 6 months of age did not reveal any behavioral abnormalities.
source: Subsequent analyses of the mice at 6 months of age did not reveal any behavioral abnormalities (Ehinger et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ehinger et al., 2020.

claim: 12-month-old HTTSA mice showed no significant differences in behavior compared to WT mice.
source: Given our observation that anterograde transport and presynaptic accumulation of APP are both reduced in HTTSA mice and that APP is associated with late-onset defects, we subjected the mice to complete behavioral analysis (SHIRPA Rogers et al., 1997, open field, grip test and elevated plus Maze) when they were 12 months old, and again found no significant differences in behavior (Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: HTTSA mice between 8 and 11 weeks of age showed greater whole brain volume (4.8%).
source: HTTSA mice between 8 and 11 weeks of age showed greater whole brain volume (4.8%) affecting the hippocampus (8.5%) and the cortex (3.7%) but not the striatum.
evidence: This is supported by MRI data.

claim: HTTSA mice between 8 and 11 weeks of age showed increased hippocampus volume (8.5%).
source: HTTSA mice between 8 and 11 weeks of age showed greater whole brain volume (4.8%) affecting the hippocampus (8.5%) and the cortex (3.7%) but not the striatum.
evidence: This is supported by MRI data.

claim: HTTSA mice between 8 and 11 weeks of age showed increased cortex volume (3.7%).
source: HTTSA mice between 8 and 11 weeks of age showed greater whole brain volume (4.8%) affecting the hippocampus (8.5%) and the cortex (3.7%) but not the striatum.
evidence: This is supported by MRI data.

claim: HTTSA mice had more synapses than WT mice.
source: HTTSA mice had more synapses than WT mice but no difference in spine size (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: HTTSA mice had no difference in spine size compared to WT mice.
source: HTTSA mice had more synapses than WT mice but no difference in spine size (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: HTTSA neuronal circuits showed an increase in the number of synaptic contacts compared to WT circuits.
source: In agreement with our in vivo experiments (Figure 6C), we found an increase in the number of synaptic contacts in the HTTSA circuit (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Overexpressing APP-mCherry in WT presynaptic cortical neurons decreased synaptic contacts.
source: Overexpressing APP-mCherry in WT presynaptic cortical neurons decreased synaptic contacts, but overexpressing APP-mCherry in HTTSA presynaptic cortical neurons restored synaptic contacts back to the levels seen in WT neurons (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by synaptic contact quantification data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Overexpressing APP-mCherry in HTTSA presynaptic cortical neurons restored synaptic contacts back to the levels seen in WT neurons.
source: Overexpressing APP-mCherry in WT presynaptic cortical neurons decreased synaptic contacts, but overexpressing APP-mCherry in HTTSA presynaptic cortical neurons restored synaptic contacts back to the levels seen in WT neurons (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by synaptic contact quantification data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The presynaptic level of APP determines synapse number and can be modulated by HTT phosphorylation.
source: The presynaptic level of APP thus appears to determine synapse number and can be modulated by HTT phosphorylation; this further supports a role for the Akt-HTT-APP pathway in synapse homeostasis.
evidence: This is concluded from the APP overexpression rescue experiments.

claim: Expressing the HTT-480-SA construct in mature neurons led to an increase in synaptic contacts similar to what is observed in HTTSA neurons.
source: We found that expressing the HTT-480-SA construct in mature neurons led to an increase in synaptic contacts similar to what is observed in HTTSA neurons differentiated in microchambers (Figure 7A and C).
evidence: This is supported by synaptic contact quantification data shown in Figure 7A and C.

claim: The HTT S421A mutation has no major role in axon growth.
source: This suggests that the HTT S421A mutation has no major role in axon growth and/or that the increase of synaptic contacts seen in HTTSA neurons is not due to changes in neurodevelopment but rather results from reduced transport and accumulation of APP at the presynapses.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity of effects when HTT-480-SA is expressed in mature neurons.

claim: The increase of synaptic contacts seen in HTTSA neurons is not due to changes in neurodevelopment but rather results from reduced transport and accumulation of APP at the presynapses.
source: This suggests that the HTT S421A mutation has no major role in axon growth and/or that the increase of synaptic contacts seen in HTTSA neurons is not due to changes in neurodevelopment but rather results from reduced transport and accumulation of APP at the presynapses.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity of effects when HTT-480-SA is expressed in mature neurons.

claim: APP-mCherry overexpression in WT neurons transduced with HTT-480-WT led to a decrease in the number of synaptic contacts.
source: As in Figure 7B, APP-mCherry overexpression in WT neurons transduced with HTT-480-WT led to a decrease in the number of synaptic contacts.
evidence: This is supported by synaptic contact quantification data.

claim: APP-mCherry overexpression had no effect on synaptic contacts in neurons expressing HTT-480-SA.
source: However, it had no effect in neurons expressing HTT-480-SA, indicating that HTT dephosphorylation attenuates the effect of APP overexpression on synapse number (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by synaptic contact quantification data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: HTT dephosphorylation attenuates the effect of APP overexpression on synapse number.
source: However, it had no effect in neurons expressing HTT-480-SA, indicating that HTT dephosphorylation attenuates the effect of APP overexpression on synapse number (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by synaptic contact quantification data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Reducing anterograde axonal transport of APP either during axonal growth or in mature networks is sufficient to modulate synaptic contact number.
source: We conclude that reducing anterograde axonal transport of APP either during axonal growth or in mature networks is sufficient to modulate synaptic contact number.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined data on APP transport and synaptic contacts.

claim: APPPS1 mice express human APP at three times the level of murine APP.
source: We chose APPPS1 mice—double transgenics that bear a human APP transgene with the Swedish mutation (APPSwe) and a mutant human presenilin 1 (PS1L166P) transgene (Radde et al., 2006)—which express human APP at three times the level of murine APP and mimic familial Alzheimer's.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Radde et al., 2006.

claim: APPPS1 mice show reduced synapse density.
source: These mice show reduced synapse density (Alonso-Nanclares et al., 2013; Bittner et al., 2012; Hoe et al., 2012; Müller et al., 2017; Priller et al., 2009; Radde et al., 2006; Zou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The levels of APP in the non-post-synaptic density fraction of APPPS1/HTTSA mice were significantly lower than in APPPS1 mice at 10 months.
source: The levels of APP in the non-post-synaptic density fraction of APPPS1/HTTSA mice were significantly lower than in APPPS1 mice at 10 months (Figure 8A and B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 8A and B.

claim: There were no significant differences in Aβ levels between APPPS1 and APPPS1/HTTSA mice.
source: We found no significant differences between genotypes, indicating that loss of HTT phosphorylation has no effect on Aβ level, amyloid load, Aβ oligomer load or plaque aggregation.
evidence: This is supported by biochemical and histological measurements.

claim: There were no significant differences in amyloid load between APPPS1 and APPPS1/HTTSA mice.
source: We found no significant differences between genotypes, indicating that loss of HTT phosphorylation has no effect on Aβ level, amyloid load, Aβ oligomer load or plaque aggregation.
evidence: This is supported by biochemical and histological measurements.

claim: There were no significant differences in Aβ oligomer load between APPPS1 and APPPS1/HTTSA mice.
source: We found no significant differences between genotypes, indicating that loss of HTT phosphorylation has no effect on Aβ level, amyloid load, Aβ oligomer load or plaque aggregation.
evidence: This is supported by biochemical and histological measurements.

claim: There were no significant differences in plaque aggregation between APPPS1 and APPPS1/HTTSA mice.
source: We found no significant differences between genotypes, indicating that loss of HTT phosphorylation has no effect on Aβ level, amyloid load, Aβ oligomer load or plaque aggregation.
evidence: This is supported by biochemical and histological measurements.

claim: HTT dephosphorylation regulates presynaptic levels of APPSwe without affecting downstream Aβ production and/or accumulation.
source: These results indicate that HTT dephosphorylation regulates presynaptic levels of APPSwe without affecting downstream Aβ production and/or accumulation.
evidence: This is concluded from the differential effects on APP levels versus Aβ levels.

claim: APPPS1 mice showed lower synaptic density than WT mice.
source: As previously described for APPSwe-PS1ΔE9 mice, 5xFAD Tg mice, and APPxPS1-KI mice (Androuin et al., 2018; Koffie et al., 2009; Neuman et al., 2015), APPPS1 mice showed lower synaptic density and larger spines than WT mice (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 8C and citations.

claim: APPPS1 mice showed larger spines than WT mice.
source: As previously described for APPSwe-PS1ΔE9 mice, 5xFAD Tg mice, and APPxPS1-KI mice (Androuin et al., 2018; Koffie et al., 2009; Neuman et al., 2015), APPPS1 mice showed lower synaptic density and larger spines than WT mice (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 8C and citations.

claim: Unphosphorylatable HTT (HTTSA) significantly increased spine density in APPPS1 mice.
source: Strikingly, unphosphorylatable HTT (HTTSA) significantly increased spine density and completely rescued APPPS1-induced increase of spine size (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Unphosphorylatable HTT (HTTSA) completely rescued APPPS1-induced increase of spine size.
source: Strikingly, unphosphorylatable HTT (HTTSA) significantly increased spine density and completely rescued APPPS1-induced increase of spine size (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: HTTSA mice showed no significant changes in behavioral-neurological status compared to WT mice at 12 to 15 months of age.
source: Extensive phenotypic analysis of the HTTSA mice using a modified SHIRPA primary screen and various behavioral tests (Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1) revealed no significant changes in the behavioral-neurological status of 12 to 15 month-old HTTSA mice compared to WT mice.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: There were no significant differences in locomotor activity between WT, APPPS1, and APPPS1/HTTSA mice.
source: When we compared WT, APPPS1, and APPPS1/HTTSA mice, we found no significant differences in locomotor activity or anxiety-related behavior in the open field test (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by open field test data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: There were no significant differences in anxiety-related behavior between WT, APPPS1, and APPPS1/HTTSA mice.
source: When we compared WT, APPPS1, and APPPS1/HTTSA mice, we found no significant differences in locomotor activity or anxiety-related behavior in the open field test (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by open field test data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: APPPS1 mice took longer paths to reach the platform of the water maze.
source: As expected, APPPS1 mice took longer paths to reach the platform of the water maze (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is supported by Morris water maze data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: APPPS1/HTTSA mice performed better than APPPS1 mice in the Morris water maze, although not to the level of WT mice.
source: APPPS1/HTTSA mice performed better than APPPS1 mice, although not to the level of WT mice.
evidence: This is supported by Morris water maze data.

claim: APPPS1/HTTSA mice performed about as poorly as the APPPS1 mice in the early stages of learning (first training sessions).
source: Comparing the early and late stages of learning in the APPPS1/HTTSA mice, we found that APPPS1/HTTSA mice performed about as poorly as the APPPS1 mice in the early stages of learning (first training sessions).
evidence: This is supported by Morris water maze data comparing early and late training phases.

claim: In the late training sessions, APPPS1/HTTSA mice performed much better than APPPS1 mice and showed a substantial recovery of performance.
source: In the late training sessions, however, they performed much better than APPPS1 mice and showed a substantial recovery of performance (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is supported by Morris water maze data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: APPPS1 mice explored all quadrants of the pool equally in the probe trial.
source: APPPS1 mice explored all quadrants of the pool equally, whereas both WT and APPPS1/HTTSA mice showed a preference for the target quadrant, indicating that their memory of the platform was intact (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is supported by probe trial data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Both WT and APPPS1/HTTSA mice showed a preference for the target quadrant in the probe trial, indicating that their memory of the platform was intact.
source: APPPS1 mice explored all quadrants of the pool equally, whereas both WT and APPPS1/HTTSA mice showed a preference for the target quadrant, indicating that their memory of the platform was intact (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is supported by probe trial data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: APPPS1 mice spent similar time investigating familiar and novel objects, indicating a memory deficit.
source: APPPS1 mice spent similar time investigating familiar and novel objects, indicating a memory deficit (indicated by a memory index close to 50%).
evidence: This is supported by novel object recognition test data.

claim: APPPS1/HTTSA mice behaved as WT mice and showed a marked preference for the novel object in the novel object recognition test.
source: In contrast, APPPS1/HTTSA mice behaved as WT mice and showed a marked preference for the novel object (significantly different from the theoretical 50% random score), suggesting that unphosphorylatable HTT can mitigate the memory deficit observed in APPPS1 mice.
evidence: This is supported by novel object recognition test data.

claim: Unphosphorylatable HTT can mitigate the memory deficit observed in APPPS1 mice.
source: In contrast, APPPS1/HTTSA mice behaved as WT mice and showed a marked preference for the novel object (significantly different from the theoretical 50% random score), suggesting that unphosphorylatable HTT can mitigate the memory deficit observed in APPPS1 mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the novel object recognition test data.

claim: Blocking Akt phosphorylation at HTT S421 reduces APP presynaptic levels, improving learning and memory in APPPS1 mice.
source: We conclude that blocking Akt phosphorylation at HTT S421 reduces APP presynaptic levels, improving learning and memory in APPPS1 mice.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined data on APP levels and behavioral performance.

claim: Axonal, but not dendritic, transport of APP is regulated by Akt-phosphorylated HTT.
source: We find that axonal, but not dendritic, transport of APP is regulated by Akt-phosphorylated HTT.
evidence: This is concluded from the differential effects observed in axons versus dendrites.

claim: HTT phosphorylation at Serine 421 recruits kinesin-1 to the molecular motor complex and promotes anterograde transport of vesicles to the plus end of microtubules in axons.
source: We previously showed that HTT phosphorylation at Serine 421 recruits kinesin-1 to the molecular motor complex and promotes anterograde transport of vesicles to the plus end of microtubules in axons (Colin et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Colin et al., 2008.

claim: Modifying HTT phosphorylation affects APP transport only in axons, where all the microtubules are oriented with the plus end towards the axon terminal.
source: Given the mixed polarity of microtubules in dendrites (Kapitein and Hoogenraad, 2015; Yau et al., 2016), modifying HTT phosphorylation affects APP transport only in axons, where all the microtubules are oriented with the plus end towards the axon terminal.
evidence: This is inferred from the known microtubule polarity differences and the observed transport effects.

claim: Blocking traffic from the entorhinal cortex to the dentate gyrus greatly reduced APP levels at the synapse.
source: Our finding that the modulation of axonal transport of APP regulates synaptic APP homeostasis is in agreement with nerve ligation studies, which showed early on that blocking traffic from the entorhinal cortex to the dentate gyrus greatly reduced APP levels at the synapse (Koo et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Koo et al., 1990.

claim: Most proteins co-transported with APP are presynaptic.
source: Moreover, studies investigating the composition of APP vesicles report that most proteins co-transported with APP are presynaptic (Kohli et al., 2012; Szodorai et al., 2009) and that APP colocalizes with presynaptic proteins at the presynaptic bouton (Groemer et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kohli et al., 2012; Szodorai et al., 2009; and Groemer et al., 2011.

claim: APP colocalizes with presynaptic proteins at the presynaptic bouton.
source: Moreover, studies investigating the composition of APP vesicles report that most proteins co-transported with APP are presynaptic (Kohli et al., 2012; Szodorai et al., 2009) and that APP colocalizes with presynaptic proteins at the presynaptic bouton (Groemer et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Groemer et al., 2011.

claim: APP levels at presynaptic membranes rely on HTT-dependent axonal transport.
source: Notwithstanding the contribution of dendritic APP to synapse homeostasis (Niederst et al., 2015), our results demonstrate that APP levels at presynaptic membranes rely on HTT-dependent axonal transport.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined data on HTT-mediated transport and presynaptic APP levels.

claim: The absence of HTT phosphorylation reduced presynaptic levels of APP in APPPS1 mice.
source: The absence of HTT phosphorylation reduced presynaptic levels of APP, restored synapse number and PSD length, and attenuated memory deficits in APPPS1 mice.
evidence: This is supported by synaptosomal fractionation and electron microscopy data.

claim: The absence of HTT phosphorylation restored synapse number in APPPS1 mice.
source: The absence of HTT phosphorylation reduced presynaptic levels of APP, restored synapse number and PSD length, and attenuated memory deficits in APPPS1 mice.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data.

claim: The absence of HTT phosphorylation restored PSD length in APPPS1 mice.
source: The absence of HTT phosphorylation reduced presynaptic levels of APP, restored synapse number and PSD length, and attenuated memory deficits in APPPS1 mice.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data.

claim: The absence of HTT phosphorylation attenuated memory deficits in APPPS1 mice.
source: The absence of HTT phosphorylation reduced presynaptic levels of APP, restored synapse number and PSD length, and attenuated memory deficits in APPPS1 mice.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from Morris water maze and novel object recognition tests.

claim: HTT dephosphorylation regulates synapse homeostasis by modulating presynaptic APP levels rather than modulating APP-derived Aβ production.
source: These results suggest that HTT dephosphorylation regulates synapse homeostasis by modulating presynaptic APP levels rather than modulating APP-derived Aβ production.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of effect on Aβ levels despite effects on synapse homeostasis.

claim: Presynaptic APP contributes to synapse formation, function, and maintenance.
source: Notwithstanding the synaptic toxicity of Aβ peptides (Klementieva et al., 2017; Mucke and Selkoe, 2012; Palop and Mucke, 2010; Selkoe and Hardy, 2016; Wei et al., 2010), our findings dovetail nicely with previous results showing presynaptic APP contributes to synapse formation, function, and maintenance (Hoe et al., 2012; Müller et al., 2017; Nicolas and Hassan, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hoe et al., 2012; Müller et al., 2017; and Nicolas and Hassan, 2014.

claim: App knockout increases the number of functional synapses in vitro.
source: Our results are also in accord with reports that App knockout increases the number of functional synapses in vitro (Priller et al., 2006) and augments synaptic density in vivo, as visualized by two-photon in vivo microscopy through a cranial window (Bittner et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Priller et al., 2006 and Bittner et al., 2009.

claim: App knockout augments synaptic density in vivo.
source: Our results are also in accord with reports that App knockout increases the number of functional synapses in vitro (Priller et al., 2006) and augments synaptic density in vivo, as visualized by two-photon in vivo microscopy through a cranial window (Bittner et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bittner et al., 2009.

claim: Reducing APP presynaptic levels by blocking HTT phosphorylation increases synapse density.
source: Indeed, we found that reducing APP presynaptic levels by blocking HTT phosphorylation increases synapse density, and that this effect can be reversed by over-expressing APP in presynaptic neurons.
evidence: This is supported by synaptic contact quantification data in microfluidic devices.

claim: The effect of blocking HTT phosphorylation on synapse density can be reversed by over-expressing APP in presynaptic neurons.
source: Indeed, we found that reducing APP presynaptic levels by blocking HTT phosphorylation increases synapse density, and that this effect can be reversed by over-expressing APP in presynaptic neurons.
evidence: This is supported by APP overexpression rescue experiments.

claim: Overexpressing APP and PS1 mutations in vivo reduced synaptic density.
source: Conversely, and again in agreement with previous studies (Alonso-Nanclares et al., 2013; Bittner et al., 2012; Priller et al., 2009), we found that overexpressing APP and PS1 mutations in vivo reduced synaptic density, an effect that can be restored by HTT-mediated reduction of APP presynaptic levels, without having significant effects on Aβ levels.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Alonso-Nanclares et al., 2013; Bittner et al., 2012; and Priller et al., 2009, and the current data.

claim: The effect of overexpressing APP and PS1 mutations on synaptic density can be restored by HTT-mediated reduction of APP presynaptic levels, without having significant effects on Aβ levels.
source: Conversely, and again in agreement with previous studies (Alonso-Nanclares et al., 2013; Bittner et al., 2012; Priller et al., 2009), we found that overexpressing APP and PS1 mutations in vivo reduced synaptic density, an effect that can be restored by HTT-mediated reduction of APP presynaptic levels, without having significant effects on Aβ levels.
evidence: This is supported by the APPPS1/HTTSA mouse data.

claim: Changes in synapse homeostasis could be linked to the potential function of APP as an adhesion molecule that forms homo and/or heteromeric complexes with APP family members.
source: Although the precise physiological function of APP at the synapse remains to be elucidated, changes in synapse homeostasis could be linked to the potential function of APP as an adhesion molecule that forms homo and/or heteromeric complexes with APP family members (Müller et al., 2017; Soba et al., 2005).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning supported by citations to Müller et al., 2017 and Soba et al., 2005.

claim: Post-mortem analyses of AD patient brains report increased levels of activated Akt in mid-temporal and mid-frontal cortex soluble fractions.
source: Post-mortem analyses of AD patient brains report increased levels of activated Akt in mid-temporal and mid-frontal cortex soluble fractions (Rickle et al., 2004) as well as increased phosphorylation of Akt and of Akt substrates in membrane-bound fractions (Griffin et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rickle et al., 2004 and Griffin et al., 2005.

claim: Post-mortem analyses of AD patient brains report increased phosphorylation of Akt and of Akt substrates in membrane-bound fractions.
source: Post-mortem analyses of AD patient brains report increased levels of activated Akt in mid-temporal and mid-frontal cortex soluble fractions (Rickle et al., 2004) as well as increased phosphorylation of Akt and of Akt substrates in membrane-bound fractions (Griffin et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Griffin et al., 2005.

claim: Increased Akt activity might contribute to higher presynaptic APP levels in AD brains, leading to synapse loss and cognitive decline.
source: Our finding that inhibiting Akt-mediated HTT phosphorylation reduces APP presynaptic levels in APPPS1 mice suggests that increased Akt activity might contribute to higher presynaptic APP levels in AD brains, leading to synapse loss and cognitive decline.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the current findings and AD pathology.

claim: Knocking down the IGF-1 receptor rescues synaptic and behavioral deficits in AD mouse models.
source: Our findings may also relate to studies that show rescue of synaptic and behavioral deficits in AD mouse models by knocking down the IGF-1 receptor and inhibiting the phosphoinositide three kinase (PI3K), which are upstream of Akt-HTT (Cohen et al., 2009; Humbert et al., 2002; Martínez-Mármol et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cohen et al., 2009; Humbert et al., 2002; and Martínez-Mármol et al., 2019.

claim: Inhibiting the phosphoinositide three kinase (PI3K) rescues synaptic and behavioral deficits in AD mouse models.
source: Our findings may also relate to studies that show rescue of synaptic and behavioral deficits in AD mouse models by knocking down the IGF-1 receptor and inhibiting the phosphoinositide three kinase (PI3K), which are upstream of Akt-HTT (Cohen et al., 2009; Humbert et al., 2002; Martínez-Mármol et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cohen et al., 2009; Humbert et al., 2002; and Martínez-Mármol et al., 2019.

claim: JIP1 was identified as a scaffold for APP.
source: Prior to this study, the JNK-interacting protein 1 (JIP1) was identified as a scaffold for APP (Muresan and Muresan, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Muresan and Muresan, 2005.

claim: JIP1 determines the directionality of APP trafficking through its phosphorylation at a JNK-dependent phosphorylation site.
source: JIP1 determines the directionality of APP trafficking through its phosphorylation at a JNK-dependent phosphorylation site (Fu and Holzbaur, 2013) and could regulate amyloid-independent mechanisms of AD pathogenesis (Margevicius et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fu and Holzbaur, 2013 and Margevicius et al., 2015.

claim: JIP1 could regulate amyloid-independent mechanisms of AD pathogenesis.
source: JIP1 determines the directionality of APP trafficking through its phosphorylation at a JNK-dependent phosphorylation site (Fu and Holzbaur, 2013) and could regulate amyloid-independent mechanisms of AD pathogenesis (Margevicius et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Margevicius et al., 2015.

claim: The Akt-HTT pathway is down-regulated in HD patient brain samples and lymphoblasts as well as in HD rodent models.
source: Defects in APP trafficking could also contribute to synaptic defects observed in HD, as we found that the Akt-HTT pathway is down-regulated in HD patient brain samples and lymphoblasts as well as in HD rodent models (Colin et al., 2005; Humbert et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Colin et al., 2005 and Humbert et al., 2002.

claim: There is a notable reduction in the number of synapses particularly within the corticostriatal circuit in HD.
source: Several studies have reported a notable reduction in the number of synapses particularly within the corticostriatal circuit, which is the most profoundly affected in HD (Virlogeux et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Virlogeux et al., 2018.

claim: Subtle modifications of axonal transport of APP change synaptic levels of APP and have dramatic consequences on synapse function.
source: We find that subtle modifications of axonal transport of APP change synaptic levels of APP and have dramatic consequences on synapse function.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined in vitro and in vivo data.
